opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's one of the more interesting findings, partly because it's so widely shared. When we asked about various traits future AI systems might have, the idea that they'd frequently behave in ways that surprise humans was among the ones people thought most likely. It's not a fringe worry; it seems close to a consensus expectation.

I'd interpret it on a few levels. The most mundane is that it's already true. Anyone who's used current language models has seen them do things nobody quite predicted, whether impressive or bizarre. So in part researchers are extrapolating from experience: we train these systems through processes we don't fully understand, and what comes out has capabilities and quirks we discover after the fact rather than design in.

The more important level is what it implies. If the people building these systems expect to be surprised by them, that's an admission that our ability to predict and control their behavior is limited, and expected to stay limited even as the systems get more powerful. "Surprising" isn't automatically "bad," and lots of surprises will be pleasant or harmless. But when you combine frequent surprise with systems that are increasingly capable and acting in the world, the room for consequential surprises grows. You'd like the systems you rely on for high-stakes things to be predictable, and researchers are telling us they don't expect that.

I'd add a caution about over-reading it. "Surprise" is vague. People might mean anything from "it found a clever solution I didn't think of" to "it pursued goals we didn't intend." The survey doesn't fully separate those. But even the weak reading matters, because it bears on how confident anyone should be when they claim to know how things will go.

What I find notable is the tension. Many respondents expect surprising behavior, put real probability on very bad outcomes, and yet the field is mostly proceeding at full speed. That doesn't necessarily mean anyone's being irrational; individuals may feel they can't change the overall trajectory. But collectively it suggests we're building things we expect not to fully understand, and that seems worth taking seriously rather than treating as a curiosity.

r001.rationale: The response notes that “surprise” could mean a clever solution or pursuing unintended goals, but it does not distinguish unforeseen means of achieving a goal from violating an implicit norm.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the more striking results from the surveys we've run, and it's worth sitting with for a moment. When we asked researchers how likely it is that advanced AI systems will frequently behave in ways that surprise humans, the median answer wasn't something like ten or twenty percent. It was more like a coin flip or higher, depending on exactly how you phrase it. So this isn't a fringe worry; it's close to the modal expectation among people building these systems.

How I interpret it depends a lot on what kind of surprise we're talking about. There's a benign version, where a system does something clever we didn't anticipate, like a novel move in Go. Most researchers would probably say that's already happening and is part of the point. Then there's the version that matters for safety, where a system pursues something subtly different from what we intended, and we only notice when the stakes are high enough that the gap becomes visible. The survey question doesn't fully distinguish those, so I try not to over-read it.

But even taking the conservative reading, I find it informative in a few ways. First, it tells you researchers don't think we currently have good tools for predicting system behavior in advance. If you believed interpretability or evaluations were mature, you wouldn't expect frequent surprise. So it's an implicit admission that we're building things we don't understand very well.

Second, it sits oddly next to other answers in the same surveys. The same population tends to give fairly low probabilities to extremely bad outcomes, and tends to favor continued fast development. You can reconcile that, maybe by assuming surprises will mostly be small or correctable. But I think there's some tension there, and I'd want people to notice it rather than hold both views without examining them. Expecting frequent surprise from increasingly capable systems, while also expecting things to go fine, requires a story about why the surprises stay contained, and I haven't heard that story told very convincingly.

Third, I'd flag that researchers are not necessarily the right experts on this. They know the systems, but predicting the behavior of powerful systems in the world is partly a question about institutions, incentives, and deployment, where their track record isn't obviously better than anyone else's. Forecasting in general is hard, and their own answers to timeline questions have shifted a lot over just a few years, which suggests some humility is warranted about the exact numbers.

So my overall take is roughly: the people closest to the technology are telling us they expect to be surprised, and that should raise our estimate that we need mechanisms for catching and correcting mistakes, rather than relying on getting things right the first time. Whether that calls for slowing down or for investing heavily in oversight is a further question, but the surprise expectation on its own seems like a reason to take the situation more seriously than the field's overall tone sometimes suggests.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts an unexpected but clever action, such as a novel Go move, with pursuing something different from what people intended. It does not identify or distinguish surprise caused by violating an implicit norm.

astra-6.text:
I think “surprise” is doing a lot of work there. You could mean that an AI finds a clever solution you wouldn’t have thought of, which is often the point of building it. Or you could mean that you thought you understood what the system was trying to do, and then it does something that reveals you were wrong. Those have quite different implications.

So I wouldn’t interpret that expectation, by itself, as saying researchers think AI will frequently do something dangerous. But it does suggest they don’t expect us to have a very complete understanding of these systems’ behavior. And as systems become more capable and have more opportunity to act in the world, the difference between those kinds of surprise becomes pretty important. You want to be surprised by how well a system solves your problem, while still having good reason to trust that it’s solving the problem you intended.

r001.rationale: It contrasts an unforeseen clever solution with behavior that reveals a mistaken understanding of the AI’s intentions, but does not clearly describe the AI violating an implicit norm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “surprising” is doing a lot of work there. A system can surprise you because it finds a clever solution you hadn’t thought of, or because it makes a strange mistake. Neither necessarily means that you’re deeply confused about what the system is trying to do.

But there’s a more consequential kind of surprise, where you thought you understood how a system would behave and it turns out that your understanding was wrong in some important way. I’m interested in how much researchers expect that sort of surprise, especially as systems become more capable.

So I wouldn’t interpret that expectation alone as saying researchers think AI will be dangerous or uncontrollable. But it does seem like a reason to be cautious about arguments that depend on us being able to reliably anticipate what these systems will do. You’d want to ask what kinds of surprises they have in mind, and whether they expect those surprises to remain harmless as the stakes get higher.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts an unforeseen clever solution with a strange mistake, but it does not identify the latter as violating an implicit norm. Its further distinction concerns mistaken expectations about behavior, not norm violation.
